gotamaka.notes: The six packet suttas refer to the Gotamaka shrine near Vesālī. The candidate describes an ascetic group. AN 5.294–302:1.1 explicitly lists a gotamako among the ascetics. That form opens DPD’s gotamaka 2, ‘disciple of (another) Gotama’, which the packet omits. The group belongs with that line if it is included. The shrine still needs its own entry. AN 5.286–293 are neighboring texts.

govinda.notes: DN 19:29.2–6 identifies Disampati’s priest Govinda as Jotipāla’s father. The title passes to Jotipāla in DN 19:31.1–6, so even the bare govindo can refer to the son later in the same sutta. AN 6.54:21.1 names the son explicitly. The packet also misses govindassānusāsaneti at DN 19:47.41, again referring to the son. DN 23:35.3 is a list of discourse titles.

gundāvana.notes: MN 84 and AN 2.38 place Mahākaccāna in the same grove near Madhurā. MN 83, on the same printed page as MN 84, opens in the Maghadeva mango grove at Mithilā.

haliddavasana.notes: MN 57 and SN 46.54 both call Haliddavasana a Koliyan town. The entry’s reference to ‘another Buddha’ in the latter is misleading. The wanderers explicitly discuss Gotama’s teaching, and the mendicants take their question to him. MN 56 and SN 46.53 are neighboring texts set at Nāḷandā and Sāvatthī respectively.

hatthaka.notes: AN 1.251 names Hatthaka of Āḷavī for the four ways of gathering a following. The same biography includes the godling who needs a solid body and recalls teaching as a human in AN 3.127. DPD’s AN 3.128 points one sutta too far in this edition. AN 1.258–277, AN 2.118–129, AN 3.34, AN 3.126, AN 8.22 and SN 17.21–22 are page overlaps. The packet misses chapter summaries at AN 3.40:8.2, AN 3.132:4.2 and AN 8.30:26.1, and several mentions rendered by pronouns, e.g. AN 8.23:1.5. The story heading at Dhp 264 also contains Hatthaka, but the verse gives no identification with the lay disciple.

hatthigāma.notes: AN 8.22 and SN 35.125 identify the Vajjian village and its householder, called Ugga in the Pali and Uggata in Sujato’s translation. AN 8.21 and SN 35.124 concern Ugga of Vesālī. DN 16:4.5.2 names the village on the final journey.

hatthipāla.notes: AN 7.73:2.4 also names Hatthipāla in the list of former teachers. The entry gives AN iv.135 for this list, but the generated citations include only AN 6.54. In AN 6.54 the English places his name one verse line earlier than the Pali (20.3–4).

hemaka.notes: The placed citation reaches Bāvarī’s roster at Snp 5.1. The entry also cites verses 1084–1087, Hemaka’s own exchange with the Buddha in Snp 5.9.

hemavata.notes: Snp 1.9 names the speaker as Hemavato yakkho, and DN 32 lists him beside Sātāgira. DN 20:7.7–8 gives six thousand Himalayan spirits (hemavatā), so the entry’s claim about the chief’s personal attendance cannot be established there. The mountain sense has no candidate. The packet misses Hemavato in the discourse summary at Snp 5.19:20.5.

hiṅga.notes: MN 116:6.4 names Hiṅgū and Hiṅga separately in the list of paccekabuddhas.

hārika.notes: SN 19.16:1.5 explicitly says hāriko nāma coraghātako. Sujato translates his name as ‘Taker’, which explains the empty mention list. The place and the eyes and mouth on the headless trunk’s chest identify the entry. Its opening description ‘bandit’ should read ‘executioner’. SN 19.14–15 and SN 19.17 describe other beings.

hārita.notes: DN 20:20.9–12 places Hārita and his following among the Brahmās. It does not identify him as Vishnu as the DPD gloss does. Thag 1.29 addresses Hārita with the fletcher’s arrow simile in the elder’s entry. Thag 3.15 is the other elder’s poem (verses 261–263), for whom the packet supplies no entry. The packet misses the chapter summaries naming the first elder at Thag 1.30:2.6 and the second at Thag 3.16:5.4.

icchānaṅgala.notes: AN 5.30 identifies the Kosalan brahmin village. MN 98 and Snp 3.9 place Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja there, and SN 54.11 places the retreat there. The app’s Snp 3.9 spells the village Icchānaṅgala. SN 54.20:2.1 is a chapter summary.

indaka.notes: The conversation takes place in SN 10.1. SN 10.2 and SN 10.3 concern other spirits. SN 10.12:14.1 names Indaka in the chapter summary.

indakūṭa.notes: SN 10.1:1.2 names Indaka’s mountain near Rājagaha. SN 10.2 is set on Vulture’s Peak and SN 10.3 near Gayā.

isidatta.notes: MN 89:18.1 and SN 55.6:1.4 call Isidatta and Purāṇa the chamberlains. Both use the separately glossed compound isidattapurāṇā. SN 41.2–3 and Thag 1.120 identify the monk, for whom the packet has no entry. SN 41.10:4.1 recalls his two discourses in a summary. AN 6.119, AN 6.140 and SN 55.5 are page overlaps. AN 6.44:2.2–5 says that Purāṇa was celibate, Isidatta lived with his wife, and both were declared once-returners. The entry’s discussion of Purāṇa’s celibacy and attainment should be checked against those lines.

isipatana.notes: SN 56.11 opens at the deer park at Isipatana near Bārāṇasī. DN 16:5.8.5 describes the pilgrimage site by the first turning of the wheel without naming it. AN 3.14, AN 3.127, AN 6.59, SN 12.66, SN 22.58, SN 22.89 and SN 55.52 are neighboring texts.

jambudīpa.notes: AN 9.21 compares the people of the three realms using the derivative jambudīpakā. AN 9.20 and AN 9.22 are page overlaps. Snp 3.7:17.4 uses the synonym Jambusaṇḍa given in the entry. The packet misses the tappable jambudīpamupanītaṁ in Thig 16.1:51.2, where Sujato translates Jambudīpa as ‘Black Plum Tree Land’.

jambugāma.notes: DN 16:4.5.3–5 places Jambugāma between Ambagāma and Bhoganagara. The reference for that passage is DN ii.124 in SuttaCentral’s PTS pagination. The entry gives ii.194. Its proposed location near Campā is conjectural.

jambuka.notes: In Thag 4.5 Jambuka recalls fifty-five years of austerities, eating dung and pulling out his hair, before taking refuge in the Buddha and attaining the three knowledges. Both DPD senses describe stages of his life. The untranslated story heading at Dhp 70 also names Jambuka Thera and the verse mentions eating from a blade of grass. Thag 4.12:5.3 is a chapter summary.

jambukhādaka.notes: SN 38.1 introduces the wanderer questioning Sāriputta near Nālaka. The abbreviated dialogues continue through SN 38.16. SN 37.34 is a page overlap. SN 44.11:5.2 lists the title of Jambukhādaka’s collection.

janavasabha.notes: DN 18:9.6–10.5 supplies both names in the speaker’s own words, Janavasabha and Bimbisāra. DN 23:35.3 lists the discourse title.

janesabha.notes: DN 20 and DN 32 both name Janesabha beside Nala. Neither passage establishes the entry’s proposed identification with Janavasabha of DN 18.

jantu.notes: SN 2.25 names the godling who admonished the mendicants on the observance day. SN 2.26 concerns Rohitassa. The packet misses Jantu in the chapter summary at SN 2.30:18.2.

jantugāma.notes: Meghiya goes to this village for alms in AN 9.3 and Ud 4.1. AN 9.2 is a page overlap.

jatukaṇṇī.notes: The entry’s verses 1096–1100 are Jatukaṇṇī’s questions and the Buddha’s reply in Snp 5.12. Only the roster in Snp 5.1 is placed by the generated citations. The mention list also misses jatukaṇṇīti at Snp 5.12:3.2, where the English says only ‘replied the Buddha’.

jayasena.notes: Prince Jayasena visits the novice Aciravata in MN 125 and hosts Bhūmija (the entry’s Bhūmiya) in MN 126. MN 125:1.2–2.2 puts the Buddha at the Bamboo Grove and Aciravata in a wilderness hut. MN 124 concerns Bakkula.

jaṭābhāradvāja.notes: SN 7.6 names the brahmin who asks who can untangle the tangle. SN 7.5 and SN 7.7 concern other Bhāradvājas.

jenta.notes: DPD assigns verse 111 to its Jenta. Thag 6.9 names its speaker as Jenta Purohitaputta, the chaplain’s son, who describes giving up pride. Thig 2.2 names the nun Jentā. The packet misses the two monks in their respective chapter summaries at Thag 1.120:2.1 and Thag 6.14:7.6. The proposed identification of the chaplain’s son with Mānatthaddha in SN 7.15 is conjectural. SN 7.14 concerns a father driven out by his sons.

jeta.notes: MN 116:6.33 names Jeta and Jayanta in succession in the list of paccekabuddhas.
